title: Rabies Requires Quarantine; Pet Theft Requires Abolition
excerpt: Rabies becomes virtually fatal after symptoms appear. Pet theft and secret transport demand proof, quarantine, enforcement, and a clear abolition deadline.
body_html:
Rabies leaves no room for delay: once clinical symptoms appear, disease is virtually 100% fatal. A bite, scratch, or saliva contact with broken skin or mucous membranes demands immediate wound washing and urgent medical care—not silence, guesswork, or an uninspected animal supply chain.

World Health Organization guidance states that exposed people should wash wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek post-exposure prophylaxis before symptoms develop. Vaccination, plus rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies when indicated, can prevent death. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route; handling sick animals, uninspected slaughter, and bite attacks create different risks.

“Farm-raised” needs records, not slogans

A trade claim does not prove lawful origin. Every animal entering commerce needs traceable ownership, veterinary inspection, transport records, and quarantine compliance. Without those records, “farm-raised” remains an assertion—not evidence that stolen family companions, illegally moved animals, or diseased animals are absent.

Pet theft is not cultural debate. It is a crime against families. Operators who steal animals, use poison baits, evade checkpoints, or move animals through hidden routes place profit above ownership rights and community safety. Anger belongs on those networks and on enforcement failures that let them operate.

Separate dangers. One biosecurity gap

Household rabies exposures and commercial dog-meat transport are not automatically the same event. They show parallel vulnerabilities: delayed treatment can kill after exposure, while weak inspection and quarantine can allow unsafe animal movement and slaughter. Public health systems need transparent records, rapid reporting, and enforcement that reaches every transport route.

Vietnamese families, veterinarians, rescuers, and local reformers do not need shame. They need institutions that protect children, households, pets, and workers from preventable harm. State rabies-control targets address disease prevention. SDE’s campaign adds a clear public demand: complete abolition of the dog-meat trade by 2030.

Turn moral clarity into public pressure

Demand traceability now. Demand quarantine enforcement now. Demand protection for stolen companions and accountability for illicit operators. Then sign the national petition calling for nationwide abolition by 2030. Add your name to a public demand for action—and follow campaign updates on how that demand reaches decision-makers.
